title: Healthy Child Programme, health visiting reviews and the red book
blurb: Name the five statutory health visitor reviews, what each covers and where, the levels of support, and how the red book is used.
question: A woman 30 weeks pregnant asks when she will first meet a health visitor and what checks her baby will have in the first two years. How should the nurse explain the Healthy Child Programme?

teach.h: A universal offer for every family
teach.body: The Healthy Child Programme (HCP) is England's universal public health programme for children and families from pregnancy to 19 years. Health visitors lead it from pregnancy to age 5, then school nursing takes over. Every family gets five statutory health and development reviews, ideally from a named health visitor, with extra support in proportion to need. Plain English: every family gets the same core checks, and more help if they need it.
teach.cite: DHSC/OHID 'Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme', Part 2 (Feb 2026, updated Mar 2026)

teach.h: The five statutory health visitor reviews
teach.caption: Antenatal, new birth and 6-8 week reviews are best delivered face to face in the home by a health visitor.

rows.label: Format
values: Face to face in a suitable venue

rows.label: Tools
values: Mental health questions, feeding, safe sleep

items: Maternal mental health, using NICE's recommended identification questions.
Infant feeding: breastfeeding support, safe bottle feeding and, later, weaning.
Safe sleep and preventing sudden unexpected death in infancy.
Development: Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) and ASQ:SE at 12 months and 2-2.5 years to support professional judgement.
Looking at the baby's skin, tone and colour, noting marks, bruises or birthmarks such as Mongolian blue spots.
Completing the Personal Child Health Record (the red book) at each review.

teach.body: At 6-8 weeks the GP carries out the full physical examination of the infant, while the health visitor provides health promotion, developmental surveillance and tailored support to the family. Both happen around the same time but are different checks.
teach.cite: Delivery of the Healthy Child Programme, Part 2

teach.caption: All four levels should be available in every local authority.

items.label: Personal Child Health Record, usually red
family keeps it and brings it to every contact

teach.caption: Parents can add their own notes, such as illnesses or medicines.

items: Health visitor Rosa sees Kezia, 7 weeks, and her mother Nia at home.
Kezia is feeding well and has had her GP physical examination. Rosa discusses safe sleep and the 8-week immunisations.
Using the NICE identification questions, Nia says she has felt low and lost interest in things most days for a month.
Rosa recognises a possible perinatal mental health problem, arranges assessment and support through the GP and perinatal services, and offers targeted health visiting.

teach.text: The 6-8 week PHYSICAL examination is done by the GP, not the health visitor. And the ASQ is used at the 12-month and 2-2.5 year reviews, not at the new birth visit.

items: Five statutory reviews: antenatal (from 28 weeks), new birth (1-14 days), 6-8 weeks, 12 months (9-15 months), 2-2.5 years.
First three are face to face in the home; later two can be in Family Hubs or clinics.
ASQ (and ASQ:SE) at 12 months and 2-2.5 years; maternal mental health asked using NICE questions.
Levels: community, universal, targeted, specialist; named health visitor for continuity.
Red book = parent-held Personal Child Health Record, completed at each review.

summary: You can now list the five statutory health visitor reviews with their timing and setting, explain what each covers including maternal mental health, feeding, safe sleep and ASQ, and describe the levels of support and the red book.

A.q: Priya is 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Under the Healthy Child Programme, when should she first be offered a health visitor review?
options: At the new birth review in the first 2 weeks
A.why: The first statutory review is the antenatal review, from 28 weeks of pregnancy.

whyNot.0: The new birth review is the second review, after the antenatal one.
whyNot.1: The 6-8 week review is the third review.
whyNot.2: Health visiting begins antenatally, before midwifery discharge.

A.q: A new father asks what the 'red book' is for. Which explanation is correct?
options: A parent-held record of growth, vaccinations and reviews
A hospital record of the baby's birth and discharge
A GP-held record of the baby's illnesses
A social care record opened if there are concerns
A.why: The red book is the Personal Child Health Record, kept by parents and completed at each review with growth, vaccinations and development.

whyNot.1: Birth details may be noted, but it is not a hospital record.
whyNot.2: It is held by parents, not the GP.
whyNot.3: It is universal for every child and not a social care record.

A.q: At which health visitor reviews is the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ) used?
A.why: ASQ and ASQ:SE are used at the 12-month and 2-to-2.5-year reviews to support professional judgement.

whyNot.0: ASQ is not used at the new birth or 6-8 week reviews.
whyNot.1: ASQ assesses an infant's development, so it is not used antenatally.
whyNot.3: The 6-8 week review does not use the ASQ.

B.q: At Ella's 6-8 week check, her mother asks who examines Ella's heart, hips and eyes. Which answer is correct?
options: The health visitor at the home visit
The GP, alongside the health visitor's review
The school nurse later at entry
B.why: At 6-8 weeks the GP does the full physical examination; the health visitor provides health promotion, developmental surveillance and family support.

whyNot.0: The health visitor's role at 6-8 weeks is not the full physical examination.
whyNot.2: The midwife's newborn examination is within 72 hours, not at 6-8 weeks.

B.q: A health visitor is planning Theo's new birth review. Which approach best meets the Healthy Child Programme?
options: A telephone call within 6 weeks of birth
A clinic appointment at a Family Hub
A face-to-face home visit within 14 days
A text message with a link to online advice
B.why: The new birth review (1-14 days) is best delivered face to face in the home by a health visitor.

whyNot.0: A phone call at up to 6 weeks misses both the format and the timing.
whyNot.1: Flexible venues are for the 12-month and 2-2.5 year reviews.
whyNot.3: A text message does not meet the face-to-face standard.

B.q: A local authority offers the five reviews to all families, extra visits to families with identified concerns, and intensive coordinated care for complex needs. Which principle does this describe?
B.why: Proportionate universalism gives a universal offer to all with support scaled to need; the HCP has community, universal, targeted and specialist levels.

whyNot.1: Screening is a different public health activity.
whyNot.2: Universal credit is a welfare benefit, not a public health principle.
whyNot.3: Targeted selective support is one level within the model, not the principle covering all four levels.

C.q: At Kezia's 6-8 week review, her mother says she has felt low and tearful most days for a month and no longer enjoys things. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Reassure her that baby blues are common
Suggest she discusses it at the 12-month review
Advise her to rest more while the baby sleeps
Arrange assessment and offer targeted support
C.why: Low mood and loss of interest for a month suggest possible perinatal depression; the HCP asks about maternal mental health using NICE identification questions so it can be acted on.

whyNot.0: Baby blues settle within days; a month of symptoms needs assessment.
whyNot.1: Waiting until 12 months delays help for a possible depressive illness.
whyNot.2: Rest advice does not address possible depression.

C.q: At Mason's 12-month review, his mother has not returned the ASQ because she finds reading English difficult. What should the health visitor do?
options: Record the ASQ as declined and continue
Complete it with her using an interpreter
Ask Mason's 9-year-old sister to translate it
C.why: The review should be accessible: completing the questionnaire together with a professional interpreter keeps the developmental review valid.

whyNot.0: She has not declined; there is a language barrier to address.
whyNot.2: Children should not be used as interpreters.

C.q: At a new birth review, the health visitor notices a blue-grey mark over a baby's lower back that the parents say has been there since birth. What should she do?
options: Record it in the red book and baby's notes
Make an immediate child protection referral
Advise the parents it will need laser treatment
Ask the parents to photograph it each week
C.why: The HCP asks health visitors to observe the skin and note marks and birthmarks such as Mongolian blue spots. A birthmark present since birth should be documented so it is not later mistaken for bruising.

whyNot.1: A congenital birthmark is not a bruise; documenting it is the right step.
whyNot.2: These birthmarks do not routinely need treatment.
whyNot.3: Weekly photography is not required; accurate recording is.

reteach.title: Count to five
reteach.question: Can you name the five reviews on the fingers of one hand?

blocks.body: Thumb: before birth (from 28 weeks). Index: new birth (by 14 days). Middle: 6-8 weeks. Ring: about 1 year (9-15 months). Little finger: 2 to 2.5 years. The first three happen at home; the last two use the ASQ.

blocks.text: GP: 6-8 week physical exam. Health visitor: 6-8 week review of family, feeding, mood and development.

explain.body: Antenatal (from 28 weeks), new birth (1-14 days), 6-8 weeks, 12 months (9-15 months) and 2-2.5 years (24-30 months). All are universal.

test.q: Which age range is used for the HCP '12-month' review?
test.why: The 12-month review is delivered between 9 and 15 months.

whyNot.0: 6-9 months is before the review window.
whyNot.1: 12-18 months does not match the 9-15 month window.
whyNot.3: 10-14 months is narrower than the official window.

explain.body: Every family should have a named health visitor. Antenatal, new birth and 6-8 week reviews are best done face to face at home; the 12-month and 2-2.5 year reviews can be in Family Hubs or community venues.

test.q: Which review may be delivered at a Family Hub rather than at home?
test.why: The 12-month and 2-2.5 year reviews may be delivered flexibly in suitable venues such as Family Hubs.

whyNot.0: The antenatal review is best delivered at home.
whyNot.1: The new birth review is best delivered at home.
whyNot.2: The 6-8 week review is best delivered at home.

explain.body: Maternal mental health (NICE identification questions), infant feeding, safe sleep and SUDI prevention, development (ASQ, ASQ:SE, ELIM), observation of the skin, and completing the red book.

test.q: Which tool does the HCP specify for asking about a mother's mental health at reviews?
options: The Edinburgh scale at every review
test.why: The HCP uses NICE's recommended identification questions from the antenatal and postnatal mental health checklist.

whyNot.0: The HCP names the NICE identification questions, not this scale at every review.
whyNot.2: ASQ:SE assesses the child's social and emotional development.
whyNot.3: The HCP does not specify this tool at the 2-year review.

explain.body: Community (population-wide), universal (the five reviews), targeted (selective for higher-risk families, indicated for specific concerns) and specialist (complex needs). All should be available in each local authority.

test.q: A health visitor offers extra visits to a family after identifying a specific feeding concern. Which level of support is this?
test.why: Targeted indicated support responds to a specific concern identified in a family.

whyNot.1: Universal is the core offer of five reviews for everyone.
whyNot.2: Community level is population-wide health promotion.
whyNot.3: Specialist level is for intensive, complex care coordination.
